candidate_workflows: Assemble two to four compatible founders with technical depth and explicit responsibility for understanding users; hire only unusually effective people the team can work with closely.
Turn the initial idea into a prototype quickly, observe real users, and revise or pivot toward what they demonstrably want rather than defending the original plan.
Search neglected or painful markets, begin with smaller customers where product quality can beat sales power, and expand upward from a simple low-end product.

Before fundraising pressure arrives, clear founder and intellectual-property commitments, approach multiple investors, and compare offers by speed, dilution, control, and strings rather than prestige alone.
Keep burn, headcount, and office costs low so the company preserves time to learn from early users and freedom to reject bad deals.
title: How to Start a Startup

candidate_workflows: Model an investor's likely behavior from fund size, check size, ownership targets, and monitoring incentives before deciding whether that capital fits the startup.
Raise only what the company can productively absorb; test whether a proposed valuation would force premature hiring, narrow realistic exits, or remove strategic flexibility.
Treat investor delay, information leakage, and control demands as structural risks, and preserve competing funding and exit alternatives.
title: A Unified Theory of VC Suckage

candidate_workflows: Build technical ability through an engaging, difficult project of your own and learn alongside people whose work and tools demonstrate unusual capability.
Contribute to an existing open-source project to practice navigating real code, then start a project to practice the separate skill of choosing the problem.
Generate candidate problems from needs you experience as a user, and prefer learning environments that increase powerful skills and future options.
When seeking mentors or collaborators, demonstrate genuine interest by removing work for them instead of signaling ambition or padding a resume.
title: Undergraduation

candidate_workflows: Draft a deliberately rough first version fast, rewrite repeatedly, remove anything unnecessary, and use conversational language.
If blocked, explain the idea aloud and transcribe the explanation; start with the most important sentence rather than waiting for a complete outline.
Ask trusted readers where the draft confuses or drags, read it aloud to detect awkward or boring passages, and publish to create useful audience pressure.
title: Writing, Briefly

candidate_workflows: Use the tool and platform choices of unusually capable technical users as a leading indicator of broader adoption, while checking that their behavior reflects product quality rather than promotion.
To attract developers who can make a platform valuable, make it both open and good enough that those developers choose it for their own work.
Evaluate a platform as a system in which developer preference produces software and software, in turn, drives adoption of the underlying product.
title: Return of the Mac

candidate_workflows: Treat the first idea as provisional, schedule explicit reconsideration points, and discount attachment caused by time already invested.
Compare the current idea with alternatives by asking whether people will pay, whether the market has valuable unsolved problems, and whether the team is choosing safety over opportunity.
Prefer painful, unglamorous problems with budget and demand over ideas selected mainly for coolness; decompose the vague fear of business into concrete learnable tasks.
Train problem selection by observing customers' point of view and their existing waste, then apply technical ability to the most immediate useful problem.
title: Why Smart People Have Bad Ideas

candidate_workflows: When using PR, offer reporters a true, useful story whose framing favors the company, and match the pitch to the outlet's standards and incentives.
Trace repeated phrases, experts, and named beneficiaries across coverage to determine whether apparent momentum comes from one coordinated pitch.
Do not treat press repetition as independent market evidence; ask why each source covered the subject and separate manufactured buzz from user demand.
title: The Submarine

candidate_workflows: When institutions undervalue an unproven team, go directly to users with a product and let demonstrated value replace credentials.
Keep new-product work founder-led, fast, and close to users; treat iteration speed, incentive alignment, and team cohesion as startup advantages over internal corporate development.
Use falling startup costs to preserve founder control and evaluate acquisition as one possible outcome of a working product and proven team, not as a substitute for user value.
Assess startup career risk by life stage and reversibility, counting the learning and stronger employment signal of an honest failed attempt.
Replace school-style product ideas with observation of specific problems users already know they have.
title: Hiring is Obsolete

candidate_workflows: Organize maker work around output and autonomy rather than fixed presence, and keep the early team in an informal environment that supports concentrated work.
Protect long uninterrupted periods by reducing meetings, synchronous errands, and performative busyness; test the cost by instituting meeting-free work blocks.
Let ideas and quality control flow upward through voluntary initiative and real audience feedback instead of relying only on assignments and managerial review.
Align rewards with project ownership and market outcomes so people work on something that is creatively and economically theirs.
title: What Business Can Learn from Open Source

candidate_workflows: Compare a startup path with a corporate career by pricing the implicit value of job security, seniority, and expected promotion instead of comparing visible income alone.
Avoid using management roles as deferred rewards for strong individual work; include the politics and role mismatch created by that system in the decision.
Choose between ownership now and institutional security later with an explicit view of liquidity, control, and the random risks that can stop either path.
title: After the Ladder

candidate_workflows: Evaluate a risky startup or investment by pairing probability of success with the size of the payoff instead of judging downside or upside alone.
Treat founders' time and ideas as invested capital, then check whether equity and possible outcomes make the risk rational for founders, employees, and investors.
When diagnosing harmful wealth or influence, distinguish productive risk rewards from corruption and use transparent decision logs to attack hidden power without suppressing startup incentives.
title: Inequality and Risk

candidate_workflows: Evaluate early founders by output, energy, responsibility, and learning speed rather than age or conventional experience.
Use a short, low-capital cycle to reach a working demo, and expect the first implementation to be rewritten as it reveals the product's design.
Defer scalability, internationalization, and other hardening that would make the first version rigid unless the omitted control protects against an immediate irreversible risk.
Assess competitors by who is ahead and who can develop fastest rather than by competitor count or publicity.
Use peer practice, shared milestones, and recurring cohort contact to accelerate learning while keeping investor control light enough to preserve ownership.
Track failure risk through the mundane question of whether the team is getting enough done.
title: What I Did this Summer

candidate_workflows: Frame an initial idea as a question, implement enough to learn, and accept a wrong answer when it produces a better question or partial solution.
Create an idea-rich environment through new technology, trusted cofounder conversations, and a together-alone-together rhythm of discussion, reflection, and critique.
Start with a problem you find intolerable, combine habits from distant fields, and look for things people already use despite obvious breakage.
Before committing, ask whether people will pay; then explore making an expensive product cheap, a difficult task easy, or redefining the problem around the outcome users actually need.
Preserve exit optionality by building something valuable to multiple possible acquirers rather than depending on one buyer.
Use enjoyable projects built with friends for yourselves as a discovery path, then test whether the result solves a broader valuable problem.
title: Ideas for Startups

candidate_workflows: Recalculate capital needs from current software, hardware, distribution, and development costs instead of accepting the check size an investor's fund needs to deploy.
Compare a large funding round with an earlier acquisition path by modeling what each does to price, control, hiring, and realistic exits.
When founder and investor risk preferences diverge, consider limited secondary liquidity that removes distracting all-or-nothing pressure while leaving most founder upside at risk.
Include regulatory and exit-market constraints when judging the right funding path rather than treating a round in isolation.
title: The Venture Capital Squeeze

candidate_workflows: Plan each round as enough capital to reach a concrete milestone that makes the next funding source rational, without overfunding the current stage.
Choose among friends and family, consulting, angels, seed firms, and venture funds by comparing speed, connections, control, legal burden, and distraction risk.
Diligence investors and terms as carefully as they diligence the startup, including reputation, board power, vesting, liquidation preference, dilution, option-pool changes, and downside provisions.
Keep pursuing alternatives until money is received; use investor competition to prevent delay and never treat verbal interest or a term sheet as a closed deal.
Start the next raise early enough for search and closing delays, keep burn low, and preserve enough runway to reject coercive terms.
Prioritize a working demo and user evidence over a polished plan, while answering what the product does, who needs it, market size, revenue model, and why it can win.
title: How to Fund a Startup

candidate_workflows: Remove registration, email, payment, and permission friction unless each step is required to deliver user value; when uncertain, err toward user control and generosity.
Validate a platform shift by observing spontaneous technical adoption and useful products rather than relying on a conference label or promotional narrative.
Compete from below by giving users more power or making an incumbent's expensive product cheap or free, while designing a sustainable model around the lower cost.
Adapt product and business design to the medium's natural affordances instead of importing the constraints of the previous channel.
Use broad participation plus audience selection and feedback to surface exceptional work without forcing every contribution through centralized control.
title: Web 2.0

candidate_workflows: Classify deferred tasks by whether the replacement work is more or less important, and deliberately leave errands undone when they would displace the highest-value work.
Reserve long uninterrupted blocks for hard maker work and prevent hiring, meetings, email, and synchronous requests from turning the startup into an interruption-driven organization.
Audit a busy to-do list for low-value tasks that provide the feeling of progress while avoiding the central problem.

Ask what the best available problem is and why it is not being worked on, then approach an intimidating goal through a smaller expandable project, successive difficulty, or collaborators who share the load.
title: Good and Bad Procrastination

candidate_workflows: Evaluate work over a meaningful time horizon and require both sustained enjoyment and an outcome you admire, rather than judging momentary pleasure.
Discount prestige and money as sources of preference distortion by consulting discerning peers and asking whether you would still do the work without direct pay.
Use an always-produce rule to separate practiced interest from imagined identity and to discover which work repeatedly pulls you into making tangible things.
Choose an organic career path or a separate money-and-meaning path based on certainty, tolerance for direction, risk capacity, and whether the desired work has a market.
When uncertain, prefer flexible roles and varied work that reveal what you enjoy while preserving the option to switch paths.
title: How to Do What You Love

candidate_workflows: Look for a startup-ecosystem bottleneck where a small, precisely placed input can enable many capable people to form companies that otherwise would not exist.
Evaluate a new venture by leverage and the interest of the underlying mechanism, not only by direct financial return or altruistic framing.
Separate attraction to a startup's outcome from willingness to do its mostly difficult, unglamorous operating work.
title: Why YC
